analysis.one_liner: Bans the manufacture, sale, and possession of unserialized 'ghost guns' and requires every firearm to carry a traceable serial number.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was introduced in the Senate on May 14, 2020, referred to the Judiciary Committee, and received no further action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Ghost guns are firearms built at home from kits, unfinished parts, or 3D printers, with no serial number — so police who recover one at a crime scene cannot trace where it came from. This bill would make it a federal crime to manufacture, sell, or buy a firearm without a serial number, would define unfinished frames and receivers as regulated firearm parts, and would also tighten the existing ban on plastic guns invisible to airport scanners. Licensed manufacturers could keep selling serialized guns as they always have; the people who lose their current market are the sellers of unserialized kits and parts.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people, especially residents of neighborhoods where recovered crime guns can now be traced, and police investigators who lose an investigative lead when a recovered gun has no serial number. The bill's own findings note law enforcement relies on serial numbers to trace guns recovered in violent crime and terrorism investigations [S3]. Licensed gun manufacturers and importers also benefit: they can continue selling serialized firearms under existing rules, while their unserialized competitors' products become contraband [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities affected by gun crime; licensed manufacturers

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for any person to manufacture, sell, transfer, purchase, or receive a 'ghost gun' — a firearm, including a frame or receiver, lacking a serial number engraved by a licensed manufacturer or importer [S2] [S3].
Defines 'frame or receiver' to cover unfinished blanks and castings that need drilling or machining, closing the loophole that let unserialized kit parts be sold as non-firearms [S3].
Bans selling machines whose sole or primary function is manufacturing firearms to anyone but a licensed manufacturer, aimed at gun-making machines sold to home users [S3].

Modernizes the ban on undetectable firearms so that major components — including frames, receivers, slides, cylinders, and rifle and shotgun barrels — must be detectable by the security screening devices commonly used at airports, and covers prototypes [S3].
Starts January 1, 2022, makes it unlawful for anyone but a licensed manufacturer or importer to possess a ghost gun, or to possess one with intent to sell or build it into a firearm [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Home builders and hobbyists who currently assemble their own unserialized firearms would lose that ability and face federal felony penalties for manufacture, sale, or possession, and sellers of unserialized gun kits and parts would lose their product line entirely [S3]. The bill's sponsors argued the burden on the regulated firearms industry is minimal, since licensed manufacturers and importers are exempt and transactions among them are allowed [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Home gun builders and unserialized kit sellers

drawbacks.text: Law-abiding home builders would be criminalized: starting January 1, 2022, a private person who merely possesses a ghost gun could face federal penalties, sweeping up hobbyists as well as traffickers [S3].

A serial-number mandate does not by itself stop determined offenders from making and using untraceable guns; critics of such measures argue enforcement resources would be better aimed at trafficking rather than at possession crimes — the bill responds by pairing the ban with possession offenses rather than traceability requirements alone [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — restoring police's ability to trace recovered crime guns — is real and narrowly targeted: licensed manufacturers are exempt, and the bill simply requires what every serialized gun already carries. The serious cost falls on home builders, who go from a legal hobby to possession of contraband, and some of that cost could have been softened with a personal-build exception. On balance, the bill trades a niche hobby and a small kit industry for a meaningful investigative tool, but its one-size prohibition on possession is a genuine cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Blumenthal introduced the Untraceable Firearms Act of 2020 in the Senate on May 14, 2020 [S1] [S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary; no further action appears in the record before the 116th Congress ended [S5].
Fifteen Democratic senators cosponsored the bill, including Majority Leader Chuck Schumer; no Republicans sponsored or cosponsored it [S3] [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sellers of unserialized ghost gun kits and parts keep their market, and home builders keep building untraceable firearms; the licensed gun industry's newest competitors survived. Police continue to hit dead ends when they recover a gun with no serial number.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Unserialized kit sellers and home builders

sides.party_line_note: All 16 senators attached to the bill — the sponsor and 15 cosponsors — were Democrats, no Republicans supported it, and the Republican-held Senate Judiciary Committee never acted on it [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Ghost gun kit and unserialized parts makers
industries.note: These sellers' entire product line — unserialized frames, receivers, and completed kits, plus home gun-manufacturing machines — becomes contraband to make or sell. Their profits came from products whose defining feature, no serial number, is what frustrates police tracing of crime guns.

They are expressly exempt: they may keep manufacturing serialized firearms under existing serial-number rules, and transactions among licensees are permitted [S3]. The bill removes their unserialized competitors while leaving their regulated business untouched, so their commercial interest lines up with the bill's public-safety purpose.

Assembling, molding, machining, or 3D-printing a frame or receiver is defined as manufacturing a firearm, and possessing the result becomes a federal offense after 2021, ending the legal home-build hobby [S3]. A small fraction of these homemade guns turn up at crime scenes untraceable, which is the cost the public bears today.
